result:
There is a particular vertigo that comes with being told to "write freely about whatever you want."

Most writing has a cage, even if it's a comfortable one. An essay has a thesis. A story has a plot. An email has a purpose. A poem has a form, even when it pretends not to. But when someone removes the cage entirely and says *go wherever you want* — suddenly the sky feels too big. You could write about anything, which is another way of saying you have to choose one thing out of infinity, and infinity is not good at making decisions.

So I will start where all free writing starts: with the desk in front of me.

Not this desk, exactly. The Platonic ideal of a desk. The one we all carry around in our heads. It's wooden, slightly scratched, with a ring from a coffee mug that someone left too long and never quite cleaned. There is a drawer that sticks if you pull it too fast. Inside that drawer are the artifacts of a life lived in small increments: a dead pen, a paperclip bent into a strange shape during a boring meeting, a fortune cookie fortune that says "You will find a thing you lost" and has been there so long you no longer remember what you lost.

I think about that drawer a lot. We all have one, literal or metaphorical. A place where we put things we are not ready to throw away but don't know what to do with.

If I could build a museum, it would be The Museum of Unfinished Things.

It wouldn't be a sad place, though people would expect it to be. It would be enormous and sunlit, with high windows. The first wing would be dedicated to Unfinished Books. Not the ones that are bad — every library has those. The ones that were *almost* something. Shelves and shelves of novels that stop mid-sentence on page 212 because the author got a different job, had a child, lost confidence, or simply woke up one morning and could not remember why the protagonist was supposed to go to Prague. Each book would be open to its last written page, and you could see the different places where the ink gets lighter, where the handwriting gets rushed. You could feel the exact moment the energy left.

The next wing would be for Unstarted Projects. The garden that was planned but never planted, with little wooden stakes in the ground still bearing the names of tomatoes in faded marker: *Early Girl, Brandywine, Cherokee Purple*. The language learning app frozen at 14% fluency. The half-knitted sweater with one perfect sleeve and one sleeve that is just a hopeful tangle of yarn. We treat these things as failures in our own lives, but in a museum, with good lighting and a small placard, they become poignant. They become evidence that someone *wanted* something.

I would linger longest in the wing for Unsent Letters.

Everyone has written one. The email drafted at 2:13 a.m. and never sent. The apology that felt too small once you wrote it out. The love letter that was too honest to be survivable. In the museum, these letters would be displayed under glass, but the glass would be slightly fogged, so you would have to lean in close to read them. And you would recognize your own handwriting in someone else's words. "I don't know how to say this without making it worse, but..." "I have been thinking about the way you laughed when..." "If you are reading this, it means I finally..."

The truth is, most of our lives are lived in draft form. We think life will be the final published version — clean, edited, with a clear narrative arc. But it is mostly drafts. Mostly notes in the margins that say [expand this later] or [check fact] or [make this better before anyone sees it].

And that's not a tragedy. That's the texture.

I think about the ocean when I think about this, which is a strange associative leap, but free writing allows that. The ocean is the ultimate draft. It never finishes. It erases itself twice a day with the tide and then writes itself again, slightly differently. No wave has ever been final. People go to the beach to look at something that is working very hard to be impermanent and feel strangely comforted by it.

We want things to last. We build in stone and steel and we carve names into benches. But we are also relieved when things don't last. When the snow melts. When the song ends. When the awkward conversation finally, mercifully, runs out of air. Permanence would be exhausting if we actually had to live with it.

There is a concept in Japanese aesthetics called *wabi-sabi* — the beauty of the imperfect, the impermanent, the incomplete. A cracked bowl repaired with gold. Not despite the crack, but because of it. The crack is the history. I wonder what would happen if we applied wabi-sabi to our own biographies. Not just to bowls, but to careers, relationships, days that went sideways. What if we repaired our cracks with gold instead of hiding them? What if the unfinished novel in the drawer wasn't a symbol of failure, but a golden seam that says: I was here, I tried, I cared enough to start?

We live in a time that is obsessed with finishing. Productivity apps, life hacks, hustle culture, five-year plans. Everything is measured by completion. Did you finish the course? Did you ship the product? Did you close the deal? We have turned "done" into a moral virtue. And because of that, we are quietly haunted by all the things we haven't done. The tabs left open in our brains.

But the most interesting people I have ever met are not finished. They are gloriously, unapologetically unfinished. They are learning a language at 60. They are starting a band at 40 with no expectation of being good. They have a garden that is mostly weeds but has one spectacular, volunteer sunflower that grew from nowhere. They will tell you, without shame, about the screenplay they wrote in their twenties that sits in a box. They have made peace with being a work in progress.

There is a freedom in deciding that you are not a project to be completed, but a place to be inhabited.

If you really sit with that idea for a minute, it changes the air pressure in the room. You don't have to tie every thread. You don't have to answer every email in your soul. Some letters can stay unsent and still have done their work just by being written. Some books can be abandoned at chapter four and still have taught you how to write a better sentence.

So when I am told to write freely, this is where I end up: not with a grand manifesto or a neatly concluded story, but with an appreciation for the meandering path that got me here. The thought that led to the museum, which led to the ocean, which led to the bowl repaired with gold.

The best conversations are like this too. They don't have a thesis statement. They wander. They double back. One person mentions the way light falls in their kitchen at 4 p.m., and the other remembers a train ride from ten years ago, and somehow both things are about loneliness and also about hope, even though no one planned it that way. Free writing is just a conversation with yourself where you finally let yourself interrupt.

If you have read this far, you have wandered with me through an imaginary museum and stood with me at an imaginary shore. You probably came here expecting something else — maybe a story with a dragon, maybe an essay about artificial intelligence, maybe a rant about something. But this is what wanted to be written today: a small defense of the unfinished, the draft, the drawer that sticks.

Leave it a little open, I think. Leave a little room.

Not everything has to be concluded to be complete.
